items.raw_text: In Panton, Vermont, population 660, town clerk Kyle Rowe did it all. He crafted budgets, paid vendors, handled property tax disputes, and served as the town’s zoning supervisor and presiding elections officer. During morning office hours at the town hall—a wood-frame structure built as a church in 1858—he also fielded public records requests. Recently, he got rather busy. Panton used to get a request every year or so from a company called SmartProcure for “all purchasing records,” covering everything from road salt to computers to toilet paper. Last year, those requests started coming quarterly. Then different companies began making more specific requests, like records of every purchase related to emergency road flares. These targeted inquiries started coming monthly or more. “I’m happy to answer public records requests from people,” says Rowe, who recently moved into a position at a nearby town. “But answering it for these purposes—it feels like I’m doing unpaid opposition research on the taxpayers’ time.” Rowe’s experiences are being repeated across the US. items.title: A familiar Iranian hacking group has found a new way to cause chaos
items.raw_text: One night in October, hackers staged one of the most unusual cyber attacks in history : cranking up the temperature in refrigeration systems at hundreds of supermarkets across France and destroying millions of euros of food. Hackers have targeted commercial fridges and freezers before, but never at this scale and never in the heart of Europe. The brazen attack left cyber professionals unsure as to who might have executed such a madcap operation. But French intelligence agencies found traces of Farsi and other clues in the digital trail pointing to an elite hacking unit of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. The unit allegedly behind the hack, Shahid Kaveh, was already well known to Western intelligence agencies. Named after Mahmoud Kaveh, an Iranian commander who died during the 1980s Iran-Iraq war, it is one of several hacking units overseen by the Revolutionary Guards’ Cyber Electronic Command. items.raw_text: About six months ago, Suvrat Raju, a professor of theoretical physics at the International Centre for Theoretical Sciences in Bengaluru, India, asked a frontier AI model to solve a physics problem. He didn’t ask because he needed to know the answer. He had actually solved this particular problem already. But he had never published the solution—which made it a perfect question to test how good AI was at physics. LLMs have been trained on the whole Internet, so if a physics problem has been discussed online, it’s likely the model already knows about it and may have memorized the answer. So a fair test of AI capabilities needs to focus on problems that have never appeared online. The model didn’t answer Raju’s problem correctly, but it did better than he expected—well, enough to get him thinking that the experiment should be repeated and formalized. items.title: What's going on with the Riemann hypothesis?
items.raw_text: Last week, news broke that a mathematician had used AI to help crack one of the biggest outstanding problems in math: a proof of the Riemann hypothesis . The news follows several other major breakthroughs in math that have either been enabled by or managed entirely by large language model-based systems, a development that has left the entire field of mathematics in a state of upset. It's too early to say much about the proof itself—mathematicians are still in the process of digesting it. But we can say a little about how the proof came about, and what it tells us about the state of math. Tackling Riemann The Riemann hypothesis dates from the mid-1800s and was formulated by (you will be surprised to learn) Bernhard Riemann. There's not an obvious way to describe the details of the actual hypothesis simply, but it has implications for the distribution of prime numbers. This gives it significance for areas ranging from number theory to cryptography. items.title: How brewers can protect beers from smoke-tainted hops
items.raw_text: The 2020 Oregon wildfires burned over 1 million acres, destroyed thousands of structures, and killed 11 people. Smoke from the fires spread across the entire region; this "smoke taint" adversely affected not only local wine production , but also hops grown for beer brewing. Since the Pacific Northwest produces more than 95 percent of US hops and about 40 percent of the global supply, the potential economic impact is significant. That's why Oregon State University (OSU) scientists have been studying how brewers could offset the negative impacts of smoke taint while still incorporating affected hops in their brews. Most recently, they found that it all depends on the quantity of tainted hops that are included and when hops are added during the brewing process, according to a new paper published in the Journal of the American Society of Brewing Chemists. As previously reported , the chemistry of brewing beer is a very active area of research. For instance, in 2018 , OSU chemist Thomas Shellhammer—who also co-authored this latest paper— identified the growing popularity of " dry hopping " (adding hops after fermentation, common for pale ales) among craft brewers as the likely culprit of the exploding beer bottle phenomenon. However, the company is about to take a harder stance. Tidal announced that in the coming weeks, it will fully ban AI music because of the harm it does to human artists. Tidal debuted its initial AI policy in July 2026, which included labeling and demonetizing all songs created entirely with AI. That wasn't enough to stem the tide of AI slop, though. Over the past 90 days, Tidal reports that 43 percent of new uploads were completely AI-generated. On November 6, new uploads to Tidal hit a whopping 60 percent AI-generated. items.title: Porsche 718 Boxster prototype drive: This electric roadster is real
items.raw_text: Porsche provided flights from Albany, New York, to Los Angeles and accommodation so Ars could drive the 718 EV prototype. Ars does not accept paid editorial content. It wasn't until I was stuck in traffic on the way back from a run up and down some canyon roads that I realized just how low Porsche's upcoming all-electric 718 Boxster truly is. I was idly looking around at the other cars, doing the math on the EV adoption rate in this small sample of Los Angeles gridlock (roughly 50 percent, impressively) when I noticed that I was eye-level with a Tesla Model Y door handle. That's not particularly low for a sports car, but it's practically unheard of for an EV. Nearly all modern electric cars are built atop a skateboard-style battery pack, a stack of cells that elevates the seating position by a good 3 inches. In these SUV-heady days, that's usually not a problem, possibly even an advantage. But, in a car like this, the closer you can get your keister to the road, the greater the sensation of speed. So, for the company's first all-electric sports car, the 718 Boxster that will be fully revealed next year, Porsche engineers put the battery pack behind the driver. That powers a single motor spinning the rear wheels and creates a driving experience that both honors the simple joy of motoring in a mid-engined Boxster while pushing the 718 to new heights of power and performance. items.title: Homo erectus lived in the rainforest alongside Denisovans
items.raw_text: Homo erectus was walking around mainland Asia at least 60,000 years more recently than archaeologists thought. A handful of teeth from two caves in southern China's Guangxi Province just filled in a significant gap in the fossil record of a region that's vital to the story of how our genus, Homo , took over the world. The chemical makeup of the teeth's enamel suggests that, over the course of their lives, these Homo erectus moved across surprisingly large distances and made their living in dense tropical rainforests—an environment we'd previously assumed that only our species had ever gained a real foothold in. And one of the teeth offers a strong clue that Homo erectus probably shared this vast landscape with the Denisovans. A handful of teeth with a lot to say Baxian and Naxian are a pair of limestone caves that lie 15 kilometers apart along a karst valley corridor in southern China. University of Copenhagen paleoanthropologist Frido Welker and his colleagues unearthed a total of nine hominin teeth from among the more than 18,000 bones and fragments from non-hominin animals found there. items.raw_text: Kunstmatige intelligentie (ai) wint snel terrein in de transport- en logistieke sector. Nederlandse bedrijven behoren daarbij tot de Europese kopgroep. Dat stelt ABN Amro na onderzoek . De bank bracht ook een sectorprognose voor de tech- en mediasector uit. De terreinwinst van ai gebeurt op een moment dat de sector zowel kansen als uitdagingen ziet. Geopolitieke spanningen, zoals de oorlog rond Iran, zorgen voor hogere brandstofprijzen en verstoringen van handelsroutes. Tegelijk groeit de internationale handel, mede door investeringen in ai, energietransitie en defensie. Volgens ABN Amro Insights (sector-updates transport & logistiek) kan de transportsector hiervan profiteren. De bank verwacht een groei van 1 procent dit jaar, oplopend naar 1,5 procent in 2027 en 1 procent in 2028. Uit cijfers van het CBS blijkt dat inmiddels één op de vijf transport- en opslagbedrijven ai gebruikt. In 2022 was dat nog één op de tien. Vooral grote ondernemingen lopen voorop: meer dan 60 procent van de bedrijven met 250 medewerkers of meer zet ai in. Bij de middelgrote bedrijven met vijftig tot 250 werkzame personen ligt het percentage op 29. Gebrek aan kennis en problemen met bestaande ict-systemen remmen verdere invoering. Robots Robotisering blijft voorlopig achter. Slechts 2 procent van de transport- en opslagbedrijven gebruikt robots. Bij grote bedrijven ligt dat aandeel rond de 25 procent.
